analysis.one_liner: Caps Japanese car imports at the number of American cars sold in Japan each year.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or floor action and died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993, with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would set a hard cap on how many cars built in Japan could be imported into the United States each year. The cap would be set to match the number of American-made cars exported to and sold in Japan in the twelve months ending the previous June 30. Because American cars sell in very small numbers in Japan, the practical effect would be a drastic cut in Japanese car imports, protecting U.S. auto manufacturing jobs but raising prices and limiting choices for American car buyers.
analysis.who_benefits: U.S. automakers and their workers would gain, because fewer Japanese imports would mean more sales of domestic cars. Communities built around auto manufacturing would benefit from steadier factory employment.

how_it_helps.text: The bill caps Japanese car imports each year at the number of U.S.-built cars exported to and sold at retail in Japan during the prior base period [S2][S3].
Japan has historically been a very small market for American-built cars, so the cap would function as a sharp import quota benefiting U.S. auto manufacturers and their workforce [S2].

analysis.who_pays: American car buyers would pay the cost, through higher prices and fewer vehicle choices as Japanese imports were cut back. Companies that import and sell Japanese vehicles, including dealerships and their employees, would also lose sales.

drawbacks.text: The quota would raise car prices for American consumers, since limiting supply of imported vehicles lets sellers charge more; import restrictions on Japanese cars in the 1980s were estimated to cost consumers thousands of dollars per car in higher prices.

The one-for-one formula is extremely restrictive because U.S. car sales in Japan are tiny, so the cap could cut imports to a small fraction of current levels, disrupting dealerships, port economies, and supply arrangements [S2][S3].

Such unilateral quantitative import limits typically invite retaliation and raise trade-friction costs for other American export industries, and they can conflict with U.S. obligations under trade agreements.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would transfer money from American car buyers to domestic automakers and their workers. It would protect some U.S. manufacturing jobs, but it would do so in the most expensive way possible — by raising prices on every new-car purchase — and it risked retaliation against American exporters. Economists across the spectrum generally view this kind of quota as a cost to the public that exceeds the benefit, concentrated narrowly in one industry.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Ways and Means Committee and its Trade Subcommittee, where it sat without a hearing, markup, or vote until the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Rep. Duncan Hunter introduced the bill on January 22, 1992, with no cosponsors [S1][S4].
The House referred it to the Ways and Means Committee on January 28, 1992, which in turn sent it to the Subcommittee on Trade [S5].
No further action was taken — no subcommittee vote, no committee markup, no floor vote — and the bill died when the Congress ended [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill failed, American car buyers avoided the higher prices a Japanese import cap would have brought, and Japanese automakers and U.S. dealers of imported cars kept their market access. Domestic automakers gained nothing they had not already secured through the voluntary export restraints of the era.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill drew no cosponsors from either party, so there was no visible partisan or coalition split; it simply never advanced.

industries.note: A hard cap on Japanese imports would shift sales from imported cars to American-built ones, raising revenue and supporting factory jobs. The mechanism works by raising the price American consumers pay for cars, so the industry's gain comes at buyers' expense.

The bill directly caps imports of Japanese-built vehicles at a fraction of current sales, since American cars sell at very low volumes in Japan. Japanese firms with U.S. plants could partially shift production to avoid the cap, since it applies only to vehicles that are products of Japan.

An import quota reduces supply and choice, and prior Japanese import restraints translated into thousands of dollars in higher prices per car. Ordinary households buying vehicles bear the cost of the subsidy to domestic manufacturers.
Dealers, port workers, and shipping firms handling Japanese vehicles would lose volume as the cap slashed imports. Communities dependent on vehicle import ports would feel job losses.
